subject: chemistry-2
question: The solubility of a salt is 36 g per 100 mL of water at 20 degrees C. A student stirs 90 g of this salt into 250 mL of water at 20 degrees C until no more dissolves. Which description of the resulting solution is accurate?

options.text: Supersaturated, because the 90 g of dissolved salt exceeds the 36 g in the solubility value
Unsaturated, because additional salt would still dissolve if the mixture were stirred longer
Supersaturated, because the mixture was stirred until no further solid would dissolve
Saturated, because 250 mL of water dissolves exactly 90 g at this temperature

explanation:
Solubility is a ratio that scales with the quantity of solvent: (36 g / 100 mL) x 250 mL = 90 g, so this solution contains exactly the maximum dissolvable amount and is saturated with no excess solid present. Choices A and C confuse saturated with supersaturated; a supersaturated solution holds more solute than the equilibrium value and must be produced indirectly, typically by saturating at a higher temperature and cooling slowly without disturbance. Stirring longer cannot exceed the equilibrium limit, so choice B misattributes an equilibrium ceiling to slow kinetics.

ELI-10: The number 36 is meaningless without the phrase per 100 mL attached to it, so never compare 90 g to 36 g directly. Scale the ratio to the solvent you actually have: 250 mL is 2.5 times 100 mL, so the ceiling is 2.5 x 36 = 90 g. Adding exactly the ceiling amount gives a saturated solution, meaning it holds the maximum at that temperature and any further solid would sit undissolved. Supersaturated is a different, unstable state produced by a temperature trick, not by stirring harder or waiting longer.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
